corpora.title: IRS Circular 230 — Enrolled Agent (EA) Practice Standards

parts.title: Subpart B — Duties and Restrictions Relating to Practice Before the IRS

sections.title: Information to be furnished
sections.text:
§ 10.20 Information to be furnished.
(a) To the Internal Revenue Service.
(1) A practitioner must, on a proper and lawful request by a duly authorized officer or employee of the Internal Revenue Service, promptly submit records or information in any matter before the Internal Revenue Service unless the practitioner believes in good faith and on reasonable grounds that the records or information are privileged.
(2) Where the requested records or information are not in the possession of, or subject to the control of, the practitioner or the practitioner's client, the practitioner must promptly notify the requesting Internal Revenue Service officer or employee and the practitioner must provide any information that the practitioner has regarding the identity of any person who the practitioner believes may have possession or control of the requested records or information. The practitioner must make reasonable inquiry of his or her client regarding the identity of any person who may have possession or control of the requested records or information, but the practitioner is not required to make inquiry of any other person or independently verify any information provided by the practitioner's client regarding the identity of such persons.

(b) Interference with a proper and lawful request. A practitioner may not interfere, or attempt to interfere, with any proper and lawful effort by the Internal Revenue Service, its officers or employees, to obtain any record or information unless the practitioner believes in good faith and on reasonable grounds that the record or information is privileged.

sections.title: Knowledge of client's omission
sections.text:
§ 10.21 Knowledge of client's omission.
A practitioner who, having been retained by a client with respect to a matter administered by the Internal Revenue Service, knows that the client has not complied with the revenue laws of the United States or has made an error in or omission from any return, document, affidavit, or other paper which the client submitted or executed under the revenue laws of the United States, must advise the client promptly of the fact of such noncompliance, error, or omission. The practitioner must advise the client of the consequences as provided under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations of such noncompliance, error, or omission.

IRS SEE Exam Doctrinal Notes on § 10.21:
1. Two Mandatory Affirmative Duties: The practitioner must promptly advise the client of BOTH (a) the fact of the noncompliance, error, or omission, AND (b) the statutory/regulatory consequences under the Internal Revenue Code (e.g., accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662, civil fraud penalties under IRC § 6663, failure-to-pay interest under IRC § 6601, and extended statutes of limitations under IRC § 6501(e)).
2. What § 10.21 Does NOT Require or Permit:
   - The practitioner is NEVER permitted to unilaterally notify the IRS of the client's prior-year error or omission without the client's consent (doing so violates client confidentiality under IRC § 7216 / § 7525).
   - The practitioner cannot force the client to file an amended return (Form 1040-X or 1120-X), nor does Circular 230 § 10.21 require the practitioner to advise the client in writing (though practitioners are strongly encouraged to document the advice), nor does § 10.21 mandate automatic withdrawal unless the prior-year omission carries forward and renders the current year's tax return false or fraudulent under § 10.22 and § 10.34.

sections.title: Diligence as to accuracy
keywords: reliance on work product of others
sections.text:
§ 10.22 Diligence as to accuracy.
(a) In general. A practitioner must exercise due diligence—
(1) In preparing or assisting in the preparation of, approving, and filing tax returns, documents, affidavits, and other papers relating to Internal Revenue Service matters;
(2) In determining the correctness of oral or written representations made by the practitioner to the Department of the Treasury; and
(3) In determining the correctness of oral or written representations made by the practitioner to clients with reference to any matter administered by the Internal Revenue Service.

(b) Reliance on others. Except as modified by §§ 10.34 and 10.37, a practitioner will be presumed to have exercised due diligence for purposes of this section if the practitioner relies on the work product of another person and the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the person, taking proper account of the nature of the relationship between the practitioner and the person.

sections.title: Fees
sections.text:
§ 10.27 Fees.
(a) In general. A practitioner may not charge an unconscionable fee in connection with any matter before the Internal Revenue Service.

(b) Contingent fees.
(1) Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(2), (3), and (4) of this section, a practitioner may not charge a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any matter before the Internal Revenue Service, including the preparation or filing of an original tax return or an amended tax return or claim for refund (other than as specified below).
(2) Exception 1 — IRS Examination or Challenge: A practitioner may charge a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with the Service's examination of, or challenge to:
(i) An original tax return; or
(ii) An amended return or claim for refund or credit where the amended return or claim for refund or credit was filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving a written notice of the examination of, or a written challenge to, the original tax return.
(3) Exception 2 — Statutory Interest or Penalties: A practitioner may charge a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the Internal Revenue Service.
(4) Exception 3 — Judicial Proceedings: A practitioner may charge a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code.

(c) Definitions. For purposes of this section, a "contingent fee" is any fee that is based, in whole or in part, on whether or not a position taken on a tax return or other filing avoids challenge by the Internal Revenue Service or is sustained either by the Internal Revenue Service or in litigation. A contingent fee includes a fee that is based on a percentage of the refund reported on a return, that is based on a percentage of the taxes saved, or that otherwise depends on the specific result attained.

sections.title: Conflicting interests
sections.text:
§ 10.29 Conflicting interests.
(a) Except as provided by paragraph (b) of this section, a practitioner shall not represent a client before the Internal Revenue Service if the representation involves a conflict of interest. A conflict of interest exists if—
(1) The representation of one client will be directly adverse to another client; or
(2) There is a significant risk that the representation of one or more clients will be materially limited by the practitioner's responsibilities to another client, a former client or a third person, or by a personal interest of the practitioner.

(b) Notwithstanding the existence of a conflict of interest under paragraph (a) of this section, the practitioner may represent a client if—
(1) The practitioner reasonably believes that the practitioner will be able to provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client;
(2) The representation is not prohibited by law; and
(3) Each affected client waives the conflict of interest and gives informed consent, confirmed in writing by each affected client, at the time the existence of the conflict of interest is known by the practitioner. The confirmation may be made within a reasonable period after the informed consent, but in no event later than 30 days.

(c) Copies of the written consents must be retained by the practitioner for at least 36 months from the date of the conclusion of the representation of the affected clients, and the written consents must be provided to any officer or employee of the Internal Revenue Service on request.

sections.title: Standards with respect to tax returns and documents, affidavits and other papers
sections.text:
§ 10.34 Standards with respect to tax returns and documents, affidavits and other papers.
(a) Tax returns.
(1) A practitioner may not willfully, recklessly, or through gross incompetence—
(i) Sign a tax return or claim for refund that the practitioner knows or reasonably should know contains a position that—
(A) Lacks a reasonable basis;
(B) Is an unreasonable position as described in section 6694(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code (including the related regulations and other published guidance); or
(C) Is a willful attempt by the practitioner to understate the liability for tax or a reckless or intentional disregard of rules or regulations by the practitioner as described in section 6694(b)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code (including the related regulations and other published guidance).
(ii) Advise a client to take a position on a tax return or claim for refund, or prepare a portion of a tax return or claim for refund containing a position, that—
(A) Lacks a reasonable basis;
(B) Is an unreasonable position as described in section 6694(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code; or
(C) Is a willful attempt by the practitioner to understate the liability for tax or a reckless or intentional disregard of rules or regulations by the practitioner as described in section 6694(b)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code.

(2) Summary of IRC § 6694(a)(2) Confidence Thresholds Referenced in § 10.34(a):
- Undisclosed Tax Return Position (Non-Tax Shelter): Must be supported by "Substantial Authority" (approximately a 40% or greater likelihood of being sustained on its merits).
- Adequately Disclosed Tax Return Position (Non-Tax Shelter, disclosed on Form 8275 or Form 8275-R): Must be supported by at least a "Reasonable Basis" (approximately a 20% or greater likelihood of being sustained on its merits; significantly higher than "not frivolous").
- Tax Shelters and Reportable Transactions (IRC § 6662A): Must meet the "More Likely Than Not" standard (a greater than 50% likelihood of being sustained on its merits), regardless of whether disclosed.

(c) Advising clients on potential penalties. A practitioner must inform a client of any penalties that are reasonably likely to apply to the client with respect to a position taken on a tax return if the practitioner advised the client with respect to the position, or prepared or signed the tax return, and must inform the client of any opportunity to avoid any such penalties by disclosure.

(d) Relying on information furnished by clients. A practitioner advising a client to take a position on a tax return, document, affidavit or other paper submitted to the Internal Revenue Service, or preparing or signing a tax return as a preparer, generally may rely in good faith without verification upon information furnished by the client. The practitioner may not, however, ignore the implications of information furnished to, or actually known by, the practitioner, and must make reasonable inquiries if the information as furnished appears to be incorrect, inconsistent with an important fact or another factual assumption, or incomplete.

sections.title: Competence
sections.text:
§ 10.35 Competence.
(a) A practitioner must possess the necessary competence to engage in practice before the Internal Revenue Service. Competent practice requires the appropriate level of knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation necessary for the matter for which the practitioner is engaged.

(b) A practitioner may become competent for the matter for which the practitioner has been engaged through various methods, such as consulting with experts in the relevant area or studying the relevant law.

questions.stem: Pacific Rim Forwarding LLC, an unlicensed ocean freight forwarder, refers a new U.S. importer, Cascade Home Furnishings Inc., to licensed customs broker Maria Vance. Pacific Rim asks Vance to pay a referral commission of $35 per customs entry filed on behalf of Cascade Home Furnishings and requests that Vance send her brokerage invoices to Pacific Rim so that Pacific Rim can bundle all logistics and customs charges onto a single consolidated invoice to Cascade. Under 19 CFR § 111.36, under what exact conditions may Broker Vance legally compensate Pacific Rim Forwarding for the referral?

options.text: A licensed customs broker is strictly prohibited under all circumstances from sharing fees or paying referral compensation to an unlicensed person or freight forwarder.

Vance may compensate the freight forwarder provided she obtains prior written approval from the Center of Excellence and Expertise (CEE) Director and caps the referral fee at 10% of the brokerage charge.
Vance may compensate the freight forwarder only if Cascade purchases the goods on a Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) basis and the forwarder acts as the Importer of Record.

Vance may compensate the freight forwarder provided she notifies the importer in advance in writing of the name of the forwarder being compensated, transmits a true copy of her brokerage charges directly to the importer (unless waived in writing by the importer), and the forwarder neither controls the brokerage fees nor forbids direct communication between the broker and the importer.
Vance may compensate the freight forwarder provided the forwarder rebates at least 50% of the referral commission back to the importer as a volume discount.

questions.goldenQuote: (1) The importer is notified in advance in writing by the broker of the name of the freight forwarder who is being compensated by the broker for the referral;
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 111 -> § 111.36 (Relations with unlicensed persons)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Look for the specific regulatory exception to the general rule against fee-splitting with unlicensed persons when the unlicensed party is a freight forwarder.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Navigate to 19 CFR Part 111 -> § 111.36 and read paragraph (c) ('Compensation of freight forwarder').

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check all 5 cumulative conditions in § 111.36(c)(1)-(5): advance written notice to the importer, direct transmittal of the brokerage bill (unless waived in writing), no control of fees by the forwarder, no ban on direct communication, and NO sharing of the referral fee with the importer.

explanation.correctReasoning: While 19 CFR § 111.36(b) generally prohibits a broker from entering into fee-splitting agreements where brokerage benefits inure to an unlicensed person, § 111.36(c) carves out an explicit exception allowing a broker to compensate a freight forwarder for referring brokerage business if five strict conditions are met: (1) advance written notice to the importer identifying the forwarder being compensated; (2) direct transmission to the importer of a true copy of the brokerage charges when collected through the forwarder (unless waived in writing by the importer); (3) the forwarder does not control or prescribe brokerage fees or conditions; (4) the forwarder does not forbid direct communication between importer and broker; and (5) no part of the compensation is shared with or refunded to the importer.

distractors.A: Incorrect because 19 CFR § 111.36(c) expressly authorizes compensating a freight forwarder for referrals when the five conditions in paragraph (c) are satisfied.
distractors.B: Incorrect because CBP regulations do not require CEE Director approval or impose a 10% percentage cap on freight forwarder referral fees.
distractors.C: Incorrect because DDP terms apply to the exception in § 111.36(a) regarding employment by an unlicensed intermediary, not the referral compensation requirements in § 111.36(c).
distractors.D: CORRECT: Accurately states the cumulative requirements of 19 CFR § 111.36(c)(1)–(4).
distractors.E: Incorrect because 19 CFR § 111.36(c)(5) explicitly prohibits sharing or refunding any part of the forwarder's referral compensation to the importer or any officer/employee of the importer.

questions.stem: While reviewing shipping documents prior to filing a consumption entry for client Global Auto Parts Inc., licensed customs broker David Chen discovers an email attachment showing that the foreign seller issued two separate invoices for the same shipment: a 'Customs Invoice' for $45,000 and a secret 'Supplemental Tooling & Price Adjustment Invoice' for $30,000 that Global Auto Parts wired separately to the seller's bank account. When Chen contacts Global Auto Parts' import manager, the manager instructs Chen to file the entry declaring only the $45,000 invoice and delete the supplemental invoice email. Under 19 CFR § 111.32, what is Broker Chen legally required to do?

options.text: File the entry at $45,000 as instructed by the principal under the Power of Attorney, because the Importer of Record bears sole legal liability for valuation accuracy under 19 U.S.C. 1484.
File the entry at $45,000 to avoid General Order storage fees, and then file a Post Summary Correction (PSC) within 180 days without informing the client.

Promptly advise the client in writing of the noncompliance/omission and the required corrective action (declaring the full $75,000 transaction value), retain a copy of the written communication in his records, and refuse to file the false entry or participate in the transaction when the client refuses to correct it.
Immediately confiscate the importer's merchandise, arrest the import manager, and assess a $30,000 civil penalty on behalf of CBP.
Provide oral advice only over the telephone so that no discoverable paper trail exists, and continue filing entries for the client using the lower invoice values.

questions.goldenQuote: If a broker knows that a client has not complied with the law or has made an error in, or omission from, any document, affidavit, or other paper which the law requires the client to execute, the broker must promptly advise the client in writing of that noncompliance, error, or omission, must instruct the client on the proper corrective action required under the law, and must retain a copy of the written communication as a record under § 111.23.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 111 -> § 111.32 (False information)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): A licensed customs broker is strictly prohibited from filing any document known to be false and has an affirmative regulatory duty when discovering client noncompliance or omission.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 111 -> § 111.32 ('False information') and examine paragraphs (a), (b), and (c).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Notice that under 19 CFR § 111.32(b) and (c), the broker's advice to the client regarding noncompliance and corrective action MUST be in writing and retained as a record under § 111.23, and the broker must refuse to file when the client refuses to correct a known false declaration.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 111.32(a), a broker must never file or assist in filing any claim or document known by the broker to be false. Under § 111.32(b), when a broker knows that a client has not complied with the law or has made an error in or omission from any required document, the broker must promptly advise the client in writing of the noncompliance, error, or omission, instruct the client on the proper corrective action, and retain a copy of that written communication for 5 years under § 111.23. Furthermore, under § 111.32(c), if the client refuses to correct the known false valuation and attempts to induce the broker to file the fraudulent $45,000 invoice, the broker must refuse to file the entry, separate from the noncompliant conduct, and document the refusal/termination.

distractors.A: Filing a document known by the broker to be false violates 19 CFR § 111.32(a) and subjects the broker to license revocation and a $30,000 monetary penalty under § 111.53 and § 111.91.
distractors.B: Knowingly filing a false entry with the intent to amend it later still violates the absolute prohibition in 19 CFR § 111.32(a) against filing a known false document.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Follows the exact mandatory steps of 19 CFR § 111.32(a), (b), and (c).
distractors.D: A customs broker is a private licensee, not a federal law enforcement officer, and has no authority to confiscate cargo, make arrests, or assess CBP penalties.
distractors.E: Oral-only advice and continued participation in double-invoicing directly violate 19 CFR § 111.32(a)–(c).

questions.stem:
Atlantic Trade Brokerage Inc., a licensed corporate customs broker headquartered in Newark, NJ, relocates its customs entry record archive to a new facility and designates a new Recordkeeping Point of Contact on October 1. In addition, Atlantic Trade Brokerage is auditing its retention schedule for three categories of documents:
(1) Standard consumption entry files (CBP Form 7501, commercial invoices, packing lists);
(2) A corporate Power of Attorney (POA) that was revoked by an active client on June 15, 2024; and
(3) Records supporting a Modernized Drawback claim that was liquidated and paid on August 10, 2025.

Under 19 CFR § 111.23 (and § 190.51(f)), where must the broker's original records be maintained, within how many days must the broker notify CBP of the change in record storage location/point of contact, and what are the mandatory retention periods for these three categories of records?

options.text: Records may be stored anywhere in North America (U.S., Canada, or Mexico); notify CBP within 60 calendar days; retain entry files for 3 years from entry, revoked POAs for 2 years from revocation, and drawback records for 5 years from entry.

Records must be maintained within the customs territory of the United States; notify the Broker Management Branch within 30 calendar days of the change; retain standard entry files for 5 years from the date of entry, revoked POAs for 5 years after the date of revocation (or 5 years after the client ceases to be an active client, whichever is later), and drawback claim records for 3 years after liquidation of the drawback claim.

Records must be maintained within the customs territory of the United States; notify CBP within 10 working days of the change; retain all entry files, revoked POAs, and drawback records for 7 years from the end of the calendar year.

Records must be maintained at the port of entry where each shipment arrived; notify CBP on the Triennial Status Report only; retain entry files for 5 years from liquidation and revoked POAs permanently.

Records may be stored on foreign cloud servers outside the U.S. customs territory without domestic access; notify CBP within 30 working days; retain entry files and drawback records for 3 years from date of importation.

questions.goldenQuote: (c) Notification of change of record storage location or point of contact. Within 30 calendar days of any change to the place of retention of records or the designated recordkeeping point of contact (including name, telephone number, or email address), the broker must electronically notify the Broker Management Branch (or submit written notification if electronic transmission is unavailable) of the new location or updated contact information.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 111 -> § 111.23 (Retention of records)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the three pillars of broker recordkeeping: geographic location requirement, notification deadline for changing storage location/contact, and specific retention timelines.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 111 -> § 111.23(a), (b), and (c), and cross-reference § 190.51(f) for drawback record retention.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Original records must be kept within the U.S. customs territory; notification to the Broker Management Branch is due within 30 calendar days; entry records = 5 years from date of entry; revoked POA = 5 years from revocation or last active client date (whichever is later); drawback records = 3 years from liquidation of the drawback claim.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 111.23(a), a licensed customs broker must maintain originals of all required customs records within the customs territory of the United States. Under § 111.23(c), within 30 calendar days of any change to the place of retention of records or the designated recordkeeping point of contact, the broker must notify the Broker Management Branch. Under § 111.23(b), standard entry records must be retained for at least 5 years after the date of entry, while revoked powers of attorney must be retained for 5 years after the date of revocation or 5 years after the date the client ceases to be an 'active client' (whichever period is later). Finally, under 19 CFR § 190.51(f) (and § 163.4(b)(1)), records supporting a drawback claim must be retained for at least 3 years after liquidation of the drawback claim.

distractors.A: Incorrect on all counts: records cannot be stored outside the U.S. customs territory, notification is 30 calendar days (not 60), and entry/POA retention is 5 years.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately states the U.S. customs territory requirement, the 30-calendar-day notification window, the 5-year entry and revoked POA rules under § 111.23, and the 3-year post-liquidation drawback retention rule under § 190.51(f).
distractors.C: Incorrect because notification is 30 calendar days (not 10 working days) and CBP does not use a 7-year tax-style retention period.
distractors.D: Incorrect because national permit holders maintain records centrally within the U.S. customs territory (not at every arrival port), must notify CBP within 30 calendar days (not wait for the Triennial Status Report), and count the 5-year entry retention period from the date of entry (not liquidation).
distractors.E: Incorrect because records must be maintained within the U.S. customs territory and entry retention is 5 years from the date of entry.

questions.stem:
BioCare Imports Inc. enters two separate shipments under its continuous Basic Importation and Entry Bond (CBP Form 301):
• Shipment 1: Restricted medical laser devices with an entered value of $60,000 (and $2,400 in estimated duties/fees) that are refused admission by the FDA for failing federal radiation safety standards.
• Shipment 2: Non-restricted general ceramic tableware with an entered value of $40,000 (and $3,600 in estimated duties/fees) that is found to lack proper Country of Origin marking.

CBP timely issues a CBP Form 4647 (Notice to Mark and/or Notice to Redeliver) for both shipments, but BioCare has already sold both shipments into domestic commerce and fails to redeliver either shipment to CBP custody. Under 19 CFR § 113.62(d) and (n), within how many days after the CBP Form 4647 demand was BioCare required to redeliver the merchandise, and what are the exact Liquidated Damages assessments for Shipment 1 and Shipment 2?

options.text: 10 working days to redeliver; Liquidated Damages are $60,000 for Shipment 1 (1x value) and $40,000 for Shipment 2 (1x value).

30 calendar days to redeliver; Liquidated Damages are $180,000 for Shipment 1 (three times the total value of the restricted merchandise: 3 x $60,000) and $43,600 for Shipment 2 (one time the value of the non-restricted merchandise plus estimated duties, taxes, and fees: $40,000 + $3,600).
30 calendar days to redeliver; Liquidated Damages are $187,200 for Shipment 1 (3x value plus 3x duties) and $120,000 for Shipment 2 (3x value).
15 calendar days to redeliver; Liquidated Damages are capped at a flat $30,000 statutory penalty per shipment for both Shipment 1 and Shipment 2.
60 calendar days to redeliver; Liquidated Damages are $62,400 for Shipment 1 (1x value + duties) and $120,000 for Shipment 2 (3x value).

questions.goldenQuote: (1) Restricted, Prohibited, Alcoholic, or Quota-Class Merchandise (3x Value): If the principal defaults on the obligation to redeliver, mark, export, or destroy restricted or prohibited merchandise (including FDA/CPSC refused goods), alcoholic beverages, or quota-class merchandise, the obligors (principal and surety, jointly and severally) agree to pay liquidated damages equal to three times the total value of the merchandise (3x value) involved in the default.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 113 -> § 113.62 (Basic importation and entry bond conditions)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the Basic Importation and Entry Bond conditions in 19 CFR Part 113 for the redelivery timeframe after CBP Form 4647 and the two-tier liquidated damages formula.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 113 -> § 113.62 and read paragraphs (d) and (n)(1)–(2).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Redelivery is due within 30 calendar days of CBP Form 4647. For restricted/prohibited/alcoholic/quota-class goods (Shipment 1), liquidated damages equal 3x value (3 x $60,000 = $180,000). For non-restricted general goods (Shipment 2), liquidated damages equal 1x value PLUS estimated duties, taxes, and fees ($40,000 + $3,600 = $43,600).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 113.62(d), when CBP issues a timely demand for redelivery on CBP Form 4647, the principal (Importer of Record) must return the merchandise to CBP custody within 30 calendar days after the date of the demand. When the principal defaults on redelivery, § 113.62(n) prescribes two distinct liquidated damages formulas for which the principal and surety are jointly and severally liable: (1) Under § 113.62(n)(1), for restricted or prohibited merchandise (such as FDA-refused medical lasers), alcoholic beverages, or quota-class merchandise, liquidated damages equal three times the total value of the merchandise (3 x $60,000 = $180,000); (2) Under § 113.62(n)(2), for non-restricted general merchandise (such as unmarked ceramic tableware), liquidated damages equal the value of the merchandise PLUS the estimated duties, taxes, and fees determined to be due ($40,000 + $3,600 = $43,600).

distractors.A: Confuses the 30-calendar-day redelivery period with the 10-working-day Entry Summary period and fails to apply the 3x multiplier for restricted goods and the duty addition for non-restricted goods.
distractors.B: CORRECT: 30 calendar days for redelivery after CBP Form 4647; $180,000 (3x value) for restricted Shipment 1; $43,600 (1x value + $3,600 duties/fees) for non-restricted Shipment 2.
distractors.C: Erroneously adds 3x duties to Shipment 1 and applies the 3x restricted multiplier to non-restricted Shipment 2.
distractors.D: Confuses the 15-calendar-day entry filing period (§ 142.2) and the $30,000 broker penalty cap (§ 111.91) with CBP Form 301 bond liquidated damages.
distractors.E: Reverses the 3x and 1x+duties formulas between restricted and non-restricted merchandise and uses an incorrect 60-day redelivery window.

options.text: (1) Transmit the belated duty payment within 10 working days of receipt; (2) provide a written accounting statement within 30 calendar days of receipt; and (3) report the new employee within 10 calendar days of the hire date.

(1) Transmit the belated duty payment to the Government within 5 working days from receipt by the broker; (2) provide a written statement accounting for the excess funds within 60 calendar days of receipt (unless actual payment is made within that 60-calendar-day period); and (3) report the new employee to CBP within 30 calendar days after the new employee has been employed by the broker for 30 consecutive days.

(1) Transmit the belated duty payment within 24 hours of receipt; (2) provide a written accounting statement within 90 calendar days; and (3) report the new employee only on the next Triennial Status Report.

(1) Transmit the belated duty payment within 5 calendar days of receipt; (2) provide a written accounting statement within 30 working days of receipt; and (3) report the new employee within 60 calendar days of the hire date.

(1) Transmit the belated duty payment within 15 calendar days of receipt; (2) provide a written accounting statement once every 12 months; and (3) report only licensed employees within 30 working days.

questions.goldenQuote: Payments received by a broker from a client after the due date must be transmitted to the Government within 5 working days from receipt by the broker. Each broker must provide a written statement to a client accounting for funds received for the client from the Government, or received from a client where no payment to the Government has been made, or received from a client in excess of the Governmental or other charges properly payable as part of the client's customs business, within 60 calendar days of receipt.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 111 -> § 111.29 (Diligence in correspondence and paying monies)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Distinguish the three financial and employee reporting clocks in 19 CFR Part 111: belated duty payments received after the due date, client overpayment accounting statements, and new employee list reporting.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 111 -> § 111.29(a) for financial settlement deadlines and cross-reference § 111.28(c) for employee list reporting.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): In § 111.29(a), belatedly received duty funds must be transmitted to CBP within 5 WORKING days from receipt, while a written accounting for excess/refunded funds is due within 60 CALENDAR days of receipt. In § 111.28(c), a new employee must be reported within 30 CALENDAR days after completing 30 consecutive days of employment.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 111.29(a), payments received by a broker from a client after the due date must be transmitted to the Government within 5 working days from receipt by the broker. Furthermore, under § 111.29(a), each broker must provide a written statement to a client accounting for funds received for the client from the Government, or received from a client in excess of the Governmental or other charges properly payable, within 60 calendar days of receipt (unless actual payment of the funds is made within that 60-calendar-day period). Finally, under 19 CFR § 111.28(c), a national permit holder must report any new employees to CBP within 30 calendar days after the new employee has been employed by the broker for 30 consecutive days (and within 30 calendar days of termination for terminated employees).

distractors.A: Confuses the 5-working-day belated payment rule with the 10-working-day Entry Summary deadline and reverses the 60-day and 30-day windows.
distractors.B: CORRECT: 5 working days for belatedly received duty payments (§ 111.29(a)); 60 calendar days for written accounting of overpayments/refunds (§ 111.29(a)); and 30 calendar days after 30 consecutive days of employment for reporting new employees (§ 111.28(c)).
distractors.C: Incorrect because 24 hours, 90 calendar days, and waiting for the Triennial Status Report violate § 111.29(a) and § 111.28(c).
distractors.D: Mixes up working days and calendar days across § 111.29(a) (which specifies 5 working days and 60 calendar days).
distractors.E: Confuses the 12-month active client payment notice requirement in § 111.29(b)(2)(ii) with the 60-calendar-day overpayment accounting statement in § 111.29(a).

questions.stem: A container vessel carrying non-quota commercial machinery arrives within the port limits of Savannah, GA and lands its cargo on Monday, November 2. On Tuesday, November 3, the licensed customs broker transmits the entry documentation (CBP Form 3461 electronic equivalent) without an entry summary and without requesting an immediate time-of-entry election upon filing. On Wednesday, November 4, CBP authorizes the release of the merchandise. Wednesday, November 11 is Veterans Day (a federal holiday). Under 19 CFR § 141.68 and § 142.12, what is the 'time of entry' for this shipment, and what is the final deadline for the broker to file the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) with estimated duties attached without incurring liquidated damages?

options.text: Time of entry is Monday, November 2; the Entry Summary is due no later than Tuesday, November 17 (15 calendar days after landing).
Time of entry is Tuesday, November 3; the Entry Summary is due no later than Tuesday, November 17 (10 working days after filing CBP Form 3461).
Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4; the Entry Summary is due no later than Wednesday, November 18 (10 working days after time of entry, including Veterans Day).

Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4; the Entry Summary is due no later than Thursday, November 19 (10 working days after time of entry, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and the Veterans Day federal holiday).
Time of entry is Thursday, November 19 (when the Entry Summary is filed); the Entry Summary is due within 30 calendar days after release.

questions.goldenQuote: When the entry documentation is filed before the entry summary, the importer or broker must file the entry summary (CBP Form 7501 or ACE electronic equivalent), with estimated duties attached (or scheduled via Automated Clearinghouse / Periodic Monthly Statement), within 10 working days after the time of entry (as determined under § 141.68).
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 142 -> § 142.12 (Time for filing entry summary)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): First determine the 'time of entry' under 19 CFR § 141.68(a)(1) when CBP Form 3461 is filed without an entry summary and without a special filing-time request.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 142 -> § 142.12(b) and (c) to see the exact deadline for filing Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) after the time of entry.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Count 10 WORKING days starting on the day AFTER CBP authorizes release (Release = Wed, Nov 4 -> Day 1 = Thu, Nov 5). Exclude Sat/Sun (Nov 7–8), Wed Nov 11 (Veterans Day federal holiday), and Sat/Sun (Nov 14–15).

explanation.correctReasoning: First, under 19 CFR § 141.68(a)(1), when entry documentation (CBP Form 3461) is filed without an entry summary and the importer has not requested time of entry at filing, the 'time of entry' is the time CBP authorizes the release of the merchandise—here, Wednesday, November 4. Second, under 19 CFR § 142.12(b) and (c), the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) with estimated duties attached must be filed within 10 working days after the time of entry, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays. Counting working days starting the day after November 4: Day 1 = Thu Nov 5; Day 2 = Fri Nov 6; [Sat Nov 7 & Sun Nov 8 excluded]; Day 3 = Mon Nov 9; Day 4 = Tue Nov 10; [Wed Nov 11 excluded for Veterans Day federal holiday]; Day 5 = Thu Nov 12; Day 6 = Fri Nov 13; [Sat Nov 14 & Sun Nov 15 excluded]; Day 7 = Mon Nov 16; Day 8 = Tue Nov 17; Day 9 = Wed Nov 18; Day 10 = Thursday, November 19.

distractors.A: Confuses the 10-working-day Entry Summary deadline (§ 142.12(b)) with the 15-calendar-day initial entry filing window after landing before merchandise goes to General Order (§ 142.2(a)).
distractors.B: Erroneously uses the date CBP Form 3461 was submitted (Nov 3) as the time of entry without an importer election under § 141.68(a)(2) and fails to exclude Veterans Day.
distractors.C: Correctly identifies Wednesday, November 4 as the time of entry, but fails to exclude Wednesday, November 11 (Veterans Day federal holiday) when counting 10 working days.
distractors.D: CORRECT: Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4 (release authorization), and Day 10 of working days (excluding weekends and Veterans Day) is Thursday, November 19.
distractors.E: Confuses standard consumption entry release (§ 141.68(a)) with Immediate Delivery release (§ 141.68(c)), where time of entry is when the entry summary is filed, and states a non-existent 30-day deadline.

questions.stem: Sonora Industrial Supply Co. imports precision ball bearings from a manufacturer in Monterrey, Mexico, destined for the Port of Laredo, TX. The Mexican seller issues a commercial invoice written entirely in Spanish that states a single lump-sum CIF Laredo price in Mexican Pesos (MXN), without separately itemizing ocean/rail freight or insurance, and omits the $9,500 value of specialized hardening dies that Sonora purchased in Germany and furnished free of charge to the Mexican plant. Under 19 CFR § 141.86, which of the following statements accurately describes the legal sufficiency of this commercial invoice for CBP entry purposes?

options.text: The invoice is fully compliant because invoices from USMCA countries (Mexico and Canada) may be submitted in Spanish or French without translation, and foreign assists never need to be disclosed on a commercial invoice.

The invoice is deficient because § 141.86 requires every commercial invoice to be in the English language (or have attached an accurate English translation), to itemize all charges upon the merchandise by name and amount (including freight, insurance, commission, and packing), and to disclose all goods or services furnished for production not included in the invoice price (such as foreign-sourced dies/assists), while stating the purchase price in the currency of purchase.
The invoice is deficient solely because all commercial invoices presented to CBP must state the purchase price exclusively in U.S. Dollars (USD) converted by the foreign seller prior to shipment.
The invoice is compliant with respect to omitting the German dies, because only goods or services furnished inside the United States must be disclosed under § 141.86(a)(11).
The invoice does not need to state the port of entry, country of origin, or quantities in weights and measures if the shipment is valued under $250,000.

questions.goldenQuote: (11) All goods or services furnished for the production of the merchandise (e.g., "assists" such as dies, molds, tools, engineering work) not included in the invoice price. However, goods or services furnished in the United States are excluded.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 141 -> § 141.86 (Contents of invoice)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the mandatory data elements required on every commercial invoice presented for U.S. customs entry, including currency, itemized charges, assist disclosures, and language requirements.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 141 -> § 141.86 and inspect paragraphs (a)(5), (a)(8), (a)(11), and (d).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under § 141.86(a)(5), stating the purchase price in the currency of purchase (MXN) is actually required! However, the invoice violates § 141.86(a)(8) (unitemized freight/insurance), § 141.86(a)(11) (omission of the German dies assist), and § 141.86(d) (must be in English or have an accurate English translation attached).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 141.86(a) and (d), a commercial invoice must satisfy eleven general content requirements plus the English language rule: (1) Under § 141.86(d), the invoice and all attachments must be in the English language or have attached thereto an accurate translation into English; (2) Under § 141.86(a)(8), all charges upon the merchandise (including freight, insurance, commissions, and containers/packing) must be itemized by name and amount; (3) Under § 141.86(a)(11), all goods or services furnished for the production of the merchandise not included in the invoice price (such as the German hardening dies assist) must be set forth on the invoice (only goods/services furnished in the U.S. are excluded); and (4) Under § 141.86(a)(5), the purchase price is properly stated in the currency of purchase (here, MXN).

distractors.A: Incorrect because there is no USMCA exemption from the English translation requirement in § 141.86(d) or the assist disclosure rule in § 141.86(a)(11).
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately identifies the English translation requirement (§ 141.86(d)), itemized charges rule (§ 141.86(a)(8)), foreign assist disclosure rule (§ 141.86(a)(11)), and currency-of-purchase rule (§ 141.86(a)(5)).
distractors.C: Incorrect because § 141.86(a)(5) explicitly requires the invoice to set forth the purchase price in the currency of the purchase (CBP converts foreign currency using quarterly/daily Federal Reserve rates under 19 CFR Part 159).
distractors.D: Reverses the rule in § 141.86(a)(11): foreign assists (like the German dies) MUST be disclosed, whereas goods or services furnished in the United States are excluded.
distractors.E: Incorrect because port of entry (§ 141.86(a)(1)), quantities in weights and measures (§ 141.86(a)(4)), and country of origin (§ 141.86(a)(10)) are mandatory on all commercial invoices.

questions.stem: A cargo aircraft lands at Chicago O'Hare International Airport on May 1 carrying a commercial shipment of Swiss mechanical chronographs consigned to Horology Imports LLC. Due to a dispute between Horology Imports and its overseas lender, no customs broker is instructed to file entry documentation upon arrival. Under 19 CFR § 142.2 and § 142.3, what is the maximum period allowed after landing to file the required entry documentation (CBP Form 3461 package), what happens to the merchandise if entry is not filed within that period, and how long may the merchandise remain unclaimed before CBP is authorized to sell it at public auction?

options.text: Entry documentation must be filed within 10 working days after landing; if unentered, the merchandise is immediately forfeited to the U.S. Treasury and auctioned after 30 calendar days.

Entry documentation must be filed within 15 calendar days after landing; if unentered within 15 calendar days, the merchandise is treated as unclaimed and sent to a General Order (G.O.) warehouse to be held at the consignee's risk and expense, and if it remains unentered in General Order for 6 months from the date of importation, it may be sold at public auction or destroyed by CBP.
Entry documentation must be filed within 30 calendar days after landing; if unentered, the air carrier must return the cargo to Switzerland at the carrier's own expense within 45 days.
Entry documentation must be filed within 5 working days after landing; if unentered, the goods are placed in a Foreign Trade Zone (FTZ) where they may remain indefinitely without storage charges.
Entry documentation must be filed within 20 working days after landing; if unentered, the consignee is assessed a $30,000 broker penalty and the goods are auctioned after 1 year.

questions.goldenQuote: (c) Consequence of failure to make entry within 15 calendar days (General Order — Part 127). Any merchandise for which entry documentation is not filed within 15 calendar days after landing or in-bond arrival at the port of destination shall be treated as unclaimed and sent to a General Order (G.O.) warehouse or public store to be held at the risk and expense of the consignee.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 142 -> § 142.2 (Time for filing entry)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Distinguish the deadline for initial Entry filing after landing (§ 142.2) from the deadline for Entry Summary filing after release (§ 142.12).
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 142 -> § 142.2 and read paragraphs (a) and (c).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Initial entry documentation (§ 142.3) must be filed within 15 CALENDAR days after landing. Failure to make entry within 15 calendar days sends the cargo to a General Order (G.O.) warehouse at the consignee's risk and expense, and after 6 months in G.O. from the date of importation it becomes subject to CBP public auction.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 142.2(a), the entry documentation required by § 142.3 (CBP Form 3461, evidence of right to make entry, commercial/pro forma invoice, packing list, and bond identification) must be filed within 15 calendar days after landing from a vessel, aircraft, or vehicle (or after arrival at the port of destination for in-bond shipments). Under § 142.2(c) and Part 127, any merchandise for which entry is not filed within 15 calendar days after landing is treated as unclaimed and sent to a General Order (G.O.) warehouse to be held at the risk and expense of the consignee. Merchandise remaining in General Order for 6 months from the date of importation without entry may be sold at public auction or destroyed by CBP.

distractors.A: Confuses the 15-calendar-day initial entry window (§ 142.2(a)) with the 10-working-day Entry Summary window (§ 142.12(b)).
distractors.B: CORRECT: 15 calendar days after landing to file entry; transfer to General Order warehouse at consignee's risk and expense if unentered; subject to CBP public auction after 6 months in G.O.
distractors.C: Incorrect because the statutory pre-G.O. period is 15 calendar days (not 30), and unclaimed goods go to a G.O. warehouse at the consignee's expense.
distractors.D: Incorrect because 5 working days and automatic placement in a Foreign Trade Zone are not part of 19 CFR Part 142.
distractors.E: Confuses the carrier's 20-calendar-day G.O. notification deadline with the importer's 15-calendar-day entry filing deadline.

questions.stem:
Licensed customs broker Elena Rostova is onboarding two new commercial clients and reviewing a low-value shipment for each:
• Client 1 (Redwood Trading Corp., a Delaware corporation) executes a customs Power of Attorney (POA) authorizing Rostova to sign entry declarations on its behalf, and imports a single daily shipment of non-restricted sample plastic phone cases with an aggregate fair retail value in the country of shipment of $650.
• Client 2 (Sierra Artisan Partners, a California general partnership with three partners) executes a customs Power of Attorney in favor of Rostova, and imports a single daily shipment of Chinese-origin steel threaded rods valued at $700 that are subject to an active Antidumping Duty (AD/CVD) order.

Under 19 CFR § 141.19 (incorporating § 141.34) and § 141.4(b)(4), what are the maximum legal validity periods for the Powers of Attorney executed by Client 1 and Client 2, and which of the two shipments qualifies for duty-free entry exemption under Section 321 ($800 de minimis)?

options.text: Both POAs are valid for a maximum of 2 years; both the $650 phone case shipment and the $700 AD/CVD steel rod shipment qualify for Section 321 duty-free administrative exemption because both are valued under $800.

Client 1's corporate POA may be granted for an unlimited period of time, whereas Client 2's partnership POA is limited to a period not to exceed 2 years from the date of execution (and is automatically revoked by any change in partnership membership); furthermore, ONLY Client 1's $650 phone case shipment qualifies for the Section 321 ($800 de minimis) exemption because merchandise subject to Antidumping or Countervailing Duties (AD/CVD) is ineligible for Section 321 clearance.

Client 1's corporate POA is limited to 5 years and Client 2's partnership POA is valid indefinitely; neither shipment qualifies for Section 321 because commercial samples over $250 always require formal entry.

Client 1's corporate POA is valid indefinitely and Client 2's partnership POA is limited to 2 years, but BOTH shipments qualify for Section 321 clearance because the $800 de minimis threshold overrides all Antidumping Duty orders.
Client 1's corporate POA is limited to 3 years (until the next Triennial Status Report) and Client 2's partnership POA is limited to 1 year; only Client 2's shipment qualifies for Section 321.

questions.goldenQuote: (2) Partnership limitation (§ 141.34): A power of attorney granted by a partnership shall be limited to a period not to exceed 2 years from the date of execution, and shall state the names of all members of the partnership. Any change in the membership of the partnership automatically revokes the power of attorney.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 141 -> § 141.19 (Declaration of entry and Power of Attorney rules)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Compare the Power of Attorney validity duration for a corporation versus a general partnership, and check the statutory exclusions from the Section 321 ($800 de minimis) administrative exemption.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 141 -> § 141.19(c) for Power of Attorney duration rules, and check § 141.4(b)(4) for Section 321 ($800 de minimis) exclusions.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under § 141.19(c) (§ 141.34), a corporate POA may be granted for an unlimited period, whereas a partnership POA cannot exceed 2 years. Under § 141.4(b)(4), merchandise subject to Antidumping/Countervailing Duties (AD/CVD), quota, or alcohol/tobacco internal revenue taxes is strictly excluded from Section 321 clearance even if valued at $800 or less!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 141.19(c)(1)–(2) (incorporating § 141.34), a Power of Attorney executed by a corporation or sole proprietor may be granted for an unlimited period of time and remains valid until revoked, whereas a Power of Attorney granted by a partnership is strictly limited to a period not to exceed 2 years from the date of execution (and must list all partners, with any change in partnership membership automatically revoking the POA). Furthermore, under 19 CFR § 141.4(b)(4) (19 U.S.C. 1321(a)(2)(C)), while shipments imported by one person on one day with an aggregate fair retail value of $800 or less generally qualify for the Section 321 de minimis exemption (as with Client 1's $650 phone cases), merchandise subject to Antidumping or Countervailing Duties (AD/CVD) is explicitly excluded from Section 321 clearance and requires formal entry.

distractors.A: Incorrect because corporate POAs are not capped at 2 years, and AD/CVD merchandise is strictly ineligible for Section 321 de minimis clearance.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Corporate POA is valid for an unlimited period; partnership POA is capped at 2 years; $650 non-restricted shipment qualifies for Section 321, while $700 AD/CVD shipment is excluded from Section 321.
distractors.C: Incorrect because corporate POAs are not limited to 5 years, partnership POAs are not unlimited, and non-restricted plastic cases under $800 qualify for Section 321.
distractors.D: Correctly states the POA rules, but erroneously claims that Section 321 applies to merchandise subject to an Antidumping Duty order.
distractors.E: Incorrect on both POA durations and Section 321 eligibility.

questions.stem:
A presidential proclamation modifies the HTSUS to increase the Column 1 duty rate on certain alloy steel valves from 2.5% to 6.0% effective at 12:01 a.m. on Thursday, October 15. A container vessel carrying three separate shipments of these alloy steel valves arrives within the port limits of Los Angeles-Long Beach and lands its cargo on Tuesday, October 13:
• Shipment 1 (Standard Entry Without Entry Summary — No Filing-Time Election): On Wednesday, October 14, the broker transmits CBP Form 3461 entry documentation without an entry summary and without requesting time of entry at filing; CBP authorizes release on Thursday, October 15.
• Shipment 2 ('Live Entry' — Entry Summary Serving as Entry and Entry Summary): On Wednesday, October 14 (after the vessel has arrived within the port limits), the broker files the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) in proper form serving as both entry and entry summary with estimated duties attached; CBP authorizes physical release on Thursday, October 15.
• Shipment 3 (Immediate Delivery Procedure): Released on Wednesday, October 14 under a special permit for Immediate Delivery (CBP Form 3461), and the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) with estimated duties attached is filed on Wednesday, October 21.

Under 19 CFR § 141.68(a), (b), (c), and (e) (§ 141.69), what is the legal 'time of entry' and applicable duty rate (2.5% vs. 6.0%) for Shipment 1, Shipment 2, and Shipment 3?

options.text: All three shipments have a time of entry of Tuesday, October 13 (the date the vessel arrived within port limits) and are subject to the 2.5% duty rate.

Shipment 1's time of entry is Thursday, October 15 (when CBP authorizes release, resulting in the 6.0% rate); Shipment 2's time of entry is Wednesday, October 14 (when the live Entry Summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached after arrival within port limits, locking in the 2.5% rate); and Shipment 3's time of entry is Wednesday, October 21 (when the Entry Summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached after Immediate Delivery release, resulting in the 6.0% rate).
Shipment 1 and Shipment 3 lock in the 2.5% duty rate on Wednesday, October 14, whereas Shipment 2 is subject to the 6.0% duty rate because physical release occurred on Thursday, October 15.
All three shipments are subject to the 6.0% duty rate because CBP authorized physical cargo release for Shipments 1 and 2 on October 15 and Entry Summary for Shipment 3 was filed on October 21.
Shipment 1's time of entry is Wednesday, October 14 (2.5% rate); Shipment 2's time of entry is Thursday, October 15 (6.0% rate); and Shipment 3's time of entry is Wednesday, October 14 (2.5% rate).

questions.goldenQuote: (b) When entry summary serves as entry and entry summary. When an entry summary serves as both the entry documentation and entry summary ("live entry"), in accordance with § 142.3(b) of this chapter, the time of entry will be the time the entry summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached, provided the merchandise has arrived within the port limits.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 141 -> § 141.68 (Time of entry)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Under 19 CFR § 141.68(e) (§ 141.69), merchandise is subject to the rate of duty in effect at the legal 'time of entry', which differs depending on whether entry is made via standard CBP Form 3461, Live Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501), or Immediate Delivery.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 141 -> § 141.68 and compare paragraphs (a)(1), (b), and (c).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): For Shipment 1 (standard 3461 with no election), time of entry is when CBP authorizes release (Oct 15 -> 6.0%). For Shipment 2 (Live Entry Summary 7501 with estimated duties attached after arrival), time of entry is the time of filing (Oct 14 -> 2.5%) even though release happens the next day! For Shipment 3 (Immediate Delivery), time of entry is when the Entry Summary 7501 is filed with duties attached (Oct 21 -> 6.0%).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 141.68(e) (§ 141.69), imported merchandise is subject to the rate of duty in effect at the 'time of entry' determined under § 141.68: (1) For Shipment 1, under § 141.68(a)(1), when entry documentation (CBP Form 3461) is filed without an entry summary and without an importer request on the entry documentation for time of entry at filing, the time of entry is the time CBP authorizes release (Thursday, October 15 -> 6.0% duty rate); (2) For Shipment 2, under § 141.68(b), when an entry summary (CBP Form 7501) serves as both entry and entry summary ('live entry'), the time of entry is the time the entry summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached, provided the merchandise has arrived within the port limits (Wednesday, October 14 -> 2.5% duty rate); and (3) For Shipment 3, under § 141.68(c), when merchandise is released under the immediate delivery procedure, the time of entry is the time the entry summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached (Wednesday, October 21 -> 6.0% duty rate).

distractors.A: Vessel arrival date is not the time of entry unless the importer submits entry documentation prior to arrival AND explicitly requests arrival time on the entry documentation under § 141.68(a)(3).
distractors.B: CORRECT: Shipment 1 = Oct 15 (6.0% under § 141.68(a)(1)); Shipment 2 = Oct 14 (2.5% under § 141.68(b) live entry summary); Shipment 3 = Oct 21 (6.0% under § 141.68(c) immediate delivery).
distractors.C: Reverses the outcomes of all three procedures under § 141.68.
distractors.D: Fails to recognize that a Live Entry Summary under § 141.68(b) establishes time of entry upon filing in proper form with estimated duties attached (Oct 14), prior to CBP release authorization.
distractors.E: Incorrectly treats Immediate Delivery release on Oct 14 as the time of entry; under § 141.68(c), Immediate Delivery time of entry occurs only when the Entry Summary is filed with estimated duties attached.
