questions.stem: An entry specialist is classifying a specialized industrial liquid pump that has already been properly placed into 4-digit Heading 8413 pursuant to GRI 1. Inside Heading 8413, the tariff schedule contains several one-dash ('-') subheadings, each subdivided into multiple two-dash ('--') and three-dash ('---') subheadings. The entry specialist notices a two-dash ('--') subheading nested under a lower one-dash ('-') residual branch that appears to mention the pump's operating pressure, and wants to jump directly to that two-dash subheading without first comparing the competing one-dash ('-') subheadings at the top level. Under HTSUS General Rule of Interpretation 6 (GRI 6), what is the binding legal rule governing subheading comparisons within a 4-digit heading?

options.text: A classifier may jump directly to any 8-digit or 10-digit subheading anywhere within a 4-digit heading regardless of indent/dash level whenever the lower subheading has a lower duty rate.

For legal purposes, classification in the subheadings of a heading is determined according to the terms of those subheadings and any related subheading notes (and, mutatis mutandis, GRIs 1 through 5), on the strict understanding that ONLY subheadings at the same level (same dash/indent level) are comparable—meaning the classifier must first compare and select the proper one-dash ('-') subheading before comparing the two-dash ('--') subheadings nested underneath it.
Section and Chapter Notes cease to apply once a classifier moves from the 4-digit heading level to the 6-digit or 8-digit subheading level under GRI 6.
Under GRI 6, all subheading disputes within a 4-digit heading are automatically resolved by choosing the subheading that appears first in numerical order.
GRI 6 applies only when comparing two different 4-digit headings across two different chapters of the HTSUS.

questions.goldenQuote: 6. For legal purposes, the classification of goods in the subheadings of a heading shall be determined according to the terms of those subheadings and any related subheading notes and, mutatis mutandis, to the above rules, on the understanding that only subheadings at the same level are comparable.
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 6 (Rule 6 — Subheading Comparison at the Same Dash Level)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Once the 4-digit heading is fixed under GRIs 1–4, how do you navigate the indented 6-digit and 8-digit subheadings underneath that heading?
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 6 and read the statutory rule and the CBP Legal Interpretation Note on GRI 6.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under GRI 6, ONLY subheadings at the same dash/indent level are comparable! You must compare one-dash ('-') against one-dash ('-') first, lock in the winning one-dash branch, and only then compare the two-dash ('--') subheadings nested beneath that branch.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS General Rule of Interpretation 6 (GRI 6), for legal purposes, the classification of goods in the subheadings of a 4-digit heading shall be determined according to the terms of those subheadings and any related subheading notes and, mutatis mutandis, to GRIs 1 through 5, on the strict understanding that ONLY subheadings at the same level (i.e., the same indentation/dash level) are comparable. For the purposes of GRI 6, the relative Section, Chapter, and Subchapter Notes also apply unless the context otherwise requires. Therefore, a classifier must first compare only the one-dash ('-') subheadings within the 4-digit heading and select the governing one-dash subheading before proceeding to compare the two-dash ('--') subheadings nested underneath it.

distractors.A: Violates GRI 6's core mandate that only subheadings at the same indentation/dash level are comparable.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately states the GRI 6 rule that subheadings are compared strictly at the same dash/indent level (one-dash vs. one-dash, then two-dash vs. two-dash) using the terms of the subheadings, Subheading Notes, and Section/Chapter Notes.
distractors.C: Directly contradicts the second sentence of GRI 6, which states that 'the relative section, chapter and subchapter notes also apply, unless the context otherwise requires.'
distractors.D: Incorrect because GRIs 1 through 5 apply mutatis mutandis at each dash level, and ifGRI 3(c) is reached, it selects the subheading occurring LAST (not first) in numerical order at that same dash level.
distractors.E: GRI 6 governs 6-digit/8-digit subheading classification WITHIN a single 4-digit heading; 4-digit headings are determined using GRIs 1 through 4.

options.text: All four items are classified as toys or festive articles in Chapter 95 (Heading 9503 or 9505) because they are marketed and sold exclusively for children's play and amusement.

Under GRI 1 and Chapter 95 Note 1: Item 1 is excluded from Chapter 95 by Note 1(v) as utilitarian kitchenware and classified by constituent material in Heading 7323 (stainless steel kitchen articles); Item 2 is excluded from Chapter 95 by Note 1(e) ('Fancy dress of textiles, of chapter 61 or 62') and classified as woven wearing apparel in Chapter 62; Item 3 is excluded from Chapter 95 by Note 1(d) and classified in Heading 4202; and ONLY Item 4 is classified as a toy in Heading 9503.00.00.
Items 1 and 4 are classified in Heading 9503.00.00 as toys, while Item 2 is classified in Heading 9505 as a festive carnival article and Item 3 is classified in Heading 4202.
Item 1 is classified in Heading 7323, but Items 2, 3, and 4 are all classified in Heading 9503.00.00 pursuant to GRI 3(b).
All four items are classified in Chapter 62 as children's textile accessories under GRI 3(c).

questions.goldenQuote: (v) Tableware, kitchenware, toilet articles, carpets and other textile floor coverings, apparel, bed linen, table linen, toilet linen, kitchen linen and similar articles having a utilitarian function (classified according to their constituent material).
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI -> Chapters 84, 85 & 95 -> HTSUS Chapter 95 Note 1 & Heading 9503
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Under GRI 1, you must check Chapter 95 Note 1 exclusions FIRST before classifying any children's product as a toy in Heading 9503.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI -> Chapters 84, 85 & 95 -> HTSUS Chapter 95 Note 1 & Heading 9503.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check the three Chapter 95 Note 1 exclusions: Note 1(v) excludes kitchenware/tableware having a real utilitarian function (Item 1 -> Heading 7323 stainless steel kitchenware); Note 1(e) excludes durable textile fancy dress costumes (Item 2 -> Chapter 62 woven apparel); Note 1(d) excludes sports/toy bags of Heading 4202 (Item 3 -> Heading 4202). Only Item 4 (pretend plastic oven designed solely for amusement) classifies in Heading 9503.00.00!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS GRI 1, classification is determined legally according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes. Chapter 95 Note 1 sets forth mandatory legal exclusions from Chapter 95: (1) Under Chapter 95 Note 1(v), tableware, kitchenware, and similar articles having a utilitarian function are excluded from Chapter 95 and classified according to their constituent material—because Item 1 consists of real stainless-steel bakeware used to bake real food in an oven, it is utilitarian kitchenware of Heading 7323 even though sized and marketed for children; (2) Under Chapter 95 Note 1(e), 'Fancy dress of textiles, of chapter 61 or 62' is excluded from Chapter 95, placing Item 2 (a durable woven textile costume) in Chapter 62; (3) Under Chapter 95 Note 1(d), sports bags and other containers of Heading 4202 are excluded from Chapter 95, placing Item 3 in Heading 4202; and (4) Item 4 (a miniature non-heating plastic pretend play oven) satisfies the 'principal use for amusement' test and is classified as a toy in Heading 9503.00.00.

distractors.A: Ignores the binding legal exclusions in Chapter 95 Note 1(d), 1(e), and 1(v); marketing to children does not override Chapter 95 Legal Notes under GRI 1.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Applies Chapter 95 Note 1(v) (Item 1 -> 7323), Note 1(e) (Item 2 -> Ch. 62), Note 1(d) (Item 3 -> 4202), and Heading 9503.00.00 (Item 4).
distractors.C: Fails to apply Note 1(v) to the functional stainless-steel bakeware (Item 1) and Note 1(e) to the durable woven textile costume (Item 2).
distractors.D: Fails to apply Note 1(e) to the textile costume and Note 1(d) to the Heading 4202 bag.
distractors.E: Incorrect because stainless-steel cookware, nylon bags, and plastic toys are not articles of Chapter 62.

questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] During an IRS examination of client Horizon Logistics Inc., an IRS Revenue Agent makes a proper and lawful written request to Enrolled Agent Thomas Greene for Horizon's warehouse inventory ledgers from two years ago. Greene does not have the inventory ledgers in his possession, and Horizon's current president informs Greene that the ledgers were retained by Horizon's former outside bookkeeper, Carla Moss, after her contract ended. None of the records are legally privileged. Under Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 CFR § 10.20), what are Enrolled Agent Greene's exact obligations regarding the Revenue Agent's request?

options.text: Greene must hire a private investigator to independently verify whether Carla Moss actually possesses the ledgers and subpoena Carla Moss before responding to the IRS.

Greene must promptly notify the requesting IRS officer that neither he nor his client possesses the records, provide any information Greene has regarding the identity of the person (Carla Moss) whom he believes may have possession or control of the requested records, and make reasonable inquiry of his client regarding the identity of any person who may have possession or control, without being required to make inquiry of any other person or independently verify the client's information.
Greene may refuse to respond to the IRS request entirely because the Enrollee-Client privilege under Circular 230 permanently shields all accounting ledgers from IRS examination.
Greene must reconstruct the missing inventory ledgers from memory and submit estimated figures to the IRS without disclosing that the original ledgers are held by Carla Moss.
Greene must immediately withdraw from representing Horizon Logistics Inc. whenever a requested document is not in the practitioner's physical office.

questions.goldenQuote: The practitioner must make reasonable inquiry of his or her client regarding the identity of any person who may have possession or control of the requested records or information, but the practitioner is not required to make inquiry of any other person or independently verify any information provided by the practitioner's client regarding the identity of such persons.
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.20 (Information to be furnished)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check what Circular 230 requires when the IRS makes a proper and lawful request for non-privileged records that are not in the possession or control of the practitioner or client.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.20 and read paragraph (a)(2).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under § 10.20(a)(2), the practitioner must promptly notify the IRS officer, provide any information regarding who may have possession/control, and make reasonable inquiry OF THE CLIENT—but is explicitly NOT required to make inquiry of any other person or independently verify the client's statement!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.20(a)(1), a practitioner must promptly submit records or information upon a proper and lawful request by an IRS officer unless the practitioner believes in good faith and on reasonable grounds that the records are privileged. Under § 10.20(a)(2), where the requested records are not in the possession or control of the practitioner or the client, the practitioner must: (1) promptly notify the requesting IRS officer; (2) provide any information the practitioner has regarding the identity of any person believed to have possession or control of the records; and (3) make reasonable inquiry of the client regarding the identity of any person who may have possession or control. However, § 10.20(a)(2) expressly states that the practitioner is NOT required to make inquiry of any other person or independently verify the information provided by the client regarding the identity of such persons.

distractors.A: Directly contradicts 31 CFR § 10.20(a)(2), which states that the practitioner is not required to make inquiry of any third person or independently verify the client's information.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Tracks the exact statutory and regulatory text of 31 CFR § 10.20(a)(1)–(2).
distractors.C: Ordinary accounting and inventory ledgers are not privileged, and withholding non-privileged information without a good-faith reasonable belief of privilege violates § 10.20(a)(1).
distractors.D: Submitting fabricated or undisclosed reconstructions violates due diligence under § 10.22 and § 10.20.
distractors.E: Lack of possession of a third-party record does not require or justify withdrawal from representation.

questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Sarah Jenkins is retained by a new business client, Oakridge Landscaping LLC, to prepare its current-year federal income tax return. While reviewing the prior year's tax return (which was prepared by a different accountant) alongside Oakridge's general ledger, Jenkins discovers that the client omitted $140,000 of taxable cash landscaping receipts from the prior year's Schedule C. Under Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 CFR § 10.21), what are Jenkins' exact legal obligations upon discovering the client's prior-year omission?

options.text: Promptly notify the IRS Criminal Investigation Division in writing of the $140,000 omission and transmit copies of the client's general ledger to the IRS.
Prepare and electronically file an amended Form 1040-X for the prior year on the client's behalf immediately, even if the client refuses to sign or authorize the amended return.

Promptly advise the client of the fact of the noncompliance, error, or omission, AND advise the client of the consequences as provided under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations of such noncompliance, error, or omission (without unilaterally notifying the IRS).
Ignore the prior-year omission completely because Jenkins did not sign or prepare the prior year's tax return.
Automatically report the prior tax preparer to the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) within 15 calendar days and impound the client's accounting records.

questions.goldenQuote: A practitioner who, having been retained by a client with respect to a matter administered by the Internal Revenue Service, knows that the client has not complied with the revenue laws of the United States or has made an error in or omission from any return, document, affidavit, or other paper which the client submitted or executed under the revenue laws of the United States, must advise the client promptly of the fact of such noncompliance, error, or omission. The practitioner must advise the client of the consequences as provided under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations of such noncompliance, error, or omission.
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.21 (Knowledge of client's omission)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Compare how IRS Circular 230 handles a client's tax omission with how 19 CFR § 111.32 handles a customs client's error.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Switch to the '31 CFR Part 10' corpus tab -> Subpart B -> § 10.21 ('Knowledge of client's omission').

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under 31 CFR § 10.21, the practitioner must promptly advise the client of (1) the fact of the error/omission AND (2) the consequences under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations. The practitioner is NEVER allowed to report the client's omission to the IRS unilaterally or file an amended return without client consent!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.21 (Circular 230), a practitioner who knows that a client has not complied with the U.S. revenue laws or has made an error in or omission from any return or document submitted under the revenue laws (regardless of who prepared the prior return) has two mandatory duties: (1) promptly advise the client of the fact of such noncompliance, error, or omission; and (2) advise the client of the consequences under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations (such as accuracy-related penalties, interest, and statute of limitations implications). Circular 230 does NOT authorize the practitioner to inform the IRS without client consent, nor can a practitioner file an amended return without the taxpayer's authorization.

distractors.A: Unilaterally disclosing confidential client tax information to the IRS without a lawful summons or client consent violates IRC § 7216 and is not permitted by Circular 230 § 10.21.
distractors.B: A practitioner cannot file an amended tax return (Form 1040-X) without the client's signature and authorization.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Accurately states the two mandatory practitioner obligations under 31 CFR § 10.21.
distractors.D: 31 CFR § 10.21 applies whenever a retained practitioner discovers a client's error or omission on any submitted return, even if another preparer signed the prior-year return.
distractors.E: Circular 230 § 10.21 does not mandate reporting the prior preparer within 15 days or impounding client records (in fact, § 10.28 requires returning client records promptly upon request).

questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Elena Brooks manages a busy tax practice and delegates the depreciation schedule calculations for a commercial real estate client's Form 1065 partnership return to a junior staff accountant in her firm, resulting in an inadvertent computational misstatement on the return submitted to the IRS. Under 31 CFR § 10.22(a) and (b), in what three areas must a practitioner exercise due diligence, and under what exact circumstances will Brooks be presumed to have exercised due diligence when relying on the work product of another person?

options.text: A practitioner is strictly and unconditionally liable under Circular 230 for every arithmetic error made by an employee or specialist, and reliance on another person's work product is never permitted.

A practitioner must exercise due diligence in (1) preparing/assisting in preparing, approving, and filing tax returns and IRS documents, (2) determining the correctness of oral or written representations made to the Department of the Treasury, and (3) determining the correctness of oral or written representations made to clients regarding IRS matters; furthermore, the practitioner will be presumed to have exercised due diligence when relying on the work product of another person if the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the person, taking proper account of the nature of the relationship.

A practitioner is only required to exercise due diligence on written representations made under oath to an IRS Appeals Officer, and has no due diligence obligation regarding oral advice given to clients.
A practitioner is automatically presumed to have exercised due diligence whenever work is delegated to another person, even if the practitioner provided zero training, supervision, or evaluation.
A practitioner may rely on the work product of another person only if that other person is a licensed attorney or Certified Public Accountant who co-signs Form 2848.

questions.goldenQuote: (b) Reliance on others. Except as modified by §§ 10.34 and 10.37, a practitioner will be presumed to have exercised due diligence for purposes of this section if the practitioner relies on the work product of another person and the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the person, taking proper account of the nature of the relationship between the practitioner and the person.
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.22 (Diligence as to accuracy)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the general rule of due diligence in Circular 230 and the specific safe-harbor presumption for relying on the work product of others.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.22 and read paragraphs (a)(1)–(3) and (b).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Notice that § 10.22(a) covers BOTH oral and written representations to the Treasury AND to clients, and § 10.22(b) creates a presumption of due diligence if the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the other person.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.22(a), a practitioner must exercise due diligence in three domains: (1) preparing or assisting in the preparation of, approving, and filing tax returns, documents, affidavits, and other papers relating to IRS matters; (2) determining the correctness of oral or written representations made by the practitioner to the Department of the Treasury; and (3) determining the correctness of oral or written representations made by the practitioner to clients with reference to any matter administered by the IRS. Under § 10.22(b), a practitioner will be presumed to have exercised due diligence when relying on the work product of another person provided the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating that person, taking proper account of the nature of the relationship between the practitioner and the person.

distractors.A: Incorrect because 31 CFR § 10.22(b) explicitly provides a due diligence presumption when a practitioner reasonably engages, supervises, trains, and evaluates the person whose work product is relied upon.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately sets forth the three due diligence domains of § 10.22(a) and the four-factor reasonable-care standard for relying on others under § 10.22(b).
distractors.C: Incorrect because § 10.22(a)(2) and (3) explicitly apply to both oral AND written representations made to the Treasury and to clients.
distractors.D: Incorrect because blind delegation without reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the person forfeits the § 10.22(b) safe harbor.
distractors.E: Incorrect because § 10.22(b) applies to reliance on the work product of 'another person' (including staff accountants or appraisers) when reasonable care is used, not solely co-signing attorneys or CPAs.

options.text: All three contingent fee arrangements (Client A, Client B, and Client C) are strictly prohibited because Circular 230 bans all percentage-based contingent fees in any matter before the IRS.
All three contingent fee arrangements are permissible provided each client signs a written fee agreement in advance.

The contingent fee for Client A is strictly PROHIBITED because a practitioner may never charge a contingent fee for preparing or filing an original tax return; however, the contingent fees for Client B (services rendered in connection with an IRS examination of, or challenge to, an original tax return) and Client C (a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties) are explicitly PERMITTED under § 10.27(b)(2) and (b)(3).
Only the contingent fee for Client A (original tax return) is permitted, whereas contingent fees during IRS examinations (Client B) and penalty/interest claims (Client C) are prohibited.
Client A and Client B are prohibited, and contingent fees are allowed exclusively in U.S. Supreme Court litigation.

questions.goldenQuote: (3) Exception 2 — Statutory Interest or Penalties: A practitioner may charge a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the Internal Revenue Service.
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.27 (Fees)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Circular 230 § 10.27 establishes a general prohibition against contingent fees (such as a percentage of a refund or taxes saved), followed by three specific exceptions.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.27 and examine paragraphs (b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3), and (b)(4).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Charging a percentage of a refund on an ORIGINAL tax return (Client A) is strictly prohibited under § 10.27(b)(1). However, contingent fees ARE permitted for an IRS examination/challenge to an original return (§ 10.27(b)(2) — Client B), a claim solely regarding statutory interest or penalties (§ 10.27(b)(3) — Client C), and judicial proceedings (§ 10.27(b)(4)).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.27(b)(1) and (c), a practitioner is strictly prohibited from charging a contingent fee (including a percentage of a tax refund or taxes saved) for preparing or filing an original tax return (Client A). However, § 10.27(b)(2)–(4) carves out three specific exceptions where contingent fees ARE permitted: (1) under § 10.27(b)(2), services rendered in connection with an IRS examination of, or challenge to, an original tax return (or an amended return/claim filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving written notice of the examination/challenge) (Client B); (2) under § 10.27(b)(3), a claim for credit or refund filed solely in connection with the determination of statutory interest or penalties assessed by the IRS (Client C); and (3) under § 10.27(b)(4), any judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code.

distractors.A: Incorrect because § 10.27(b)(2)–(4) expressly permits contingent fees in IRS examinations/challenges, statutory interest/penalty refund claims, and judicial proceedings.
distractors.B: Incorrect because a client's written agreement cannot waive the absolute prohibition in § 10.27(b)(1) against charging a contingent fee for preparing an original tax return.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Client A (original Form 1040 return) is prohibited under § 10.27(b)(1), while Client B (IRS examination under § 10.27(b)(2)) and Client C (statutory interest/penalties under § 10.27(b)(3)) are permitted.
distractors.D: Reverses the rule and exceptions of 31 CFR § 10.27(b).
distractors.E: Incorrect because § 10.27(b)(2), (3), and (4) permit contingent fees in IRS examinations, penalty/interest claims, and any judicial proceeding under the IRC.

questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Diana Cho is asked to represent two former business partners, Alex and Jordan, in an IRS audit concerning the allocation of partnership losses between them—a matter in which Alex's tax position is directly adverse to Jordan's tax position. Cho reasonably believes that she can provide competent and diligent representation to both Alex and Jordan, and the dual representation is not prohibited by law. Both Alex and Jordan orally agree to waive the conflict of interest during a meeting on June 1. Under Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 CFR § 10.29), what written confirmation deadline and record-retention period must Cho satisfy to represent both clients legally?

options.text: Oral informed consent witnessed by a notary public is sufficient under Circular 230, and no written confirmation or retention period is required.

Each affected client must waive the conflict of interest and give informed consent, confirmed in writing by each affected client within a reasonable period after the informed consent, but in no event later than 30 days; furthermore, copies of the written consents must be retained by the practitioner for at least 36 months from the date of the conclusion of the representation of the affected clients.
Written confirmation of informed consent must be signed by the IRS Revenue Agent within 60 days, and the practitioner must retain the consent for 12 months from the date the conflict was discovered.
A conflict of interest involving direct adversity between two taxpayers before the IRS can never be waived under any circumstances, even with written consent.
Each affected client must confirm informed consent in writing within 90 days, and the practitioner must retain the written consents for 5 years from the filing of the partnership return.

questions.goldenQuote: (3) Each affected client waives the conflict of interest and gives informed consent, confirmed in writing by each affected client, at the time the existence of the conflict of interest is known by the practitioner. The confirmation may be made within a reasonable period after the informed consent, but in no event later than 30 days.
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.29 (Conflicting interests)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the exact conditions under which a practitioner may represent clients despite a conflict of interest, focusing on the two numeric timeframes in § 10.29.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.29 and read paragraphs (b)(3) and (c).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Memorize the 30-day / 36-month pair in § 10.29: informed consent must be confirmed in writing by EACH affected client within at most 30 days, and the practitioner must retain copies of the written consents for at least 36 months from the date of the CONCLUSION of the representation!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.29(a) and (b), when a conflict of interest exists, a practitioner may represent the affected clients ONLY if three cumulative conditions are met: (1) the practitioner reasonably believes they can provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client; (2) the representation is not prohibited by law; and (3) each affected client waives the conflict and gives informed consent, confirmed in writing by each affected client at the time the conflict is known (with the written confirmation made within a reasonable period after the informed consent, but in no event later than 30 days). Furthermore, under § 10.29(c), copies of the written consents must be retained by the practitioner for at least 36 months from the date of the conclusion of the representation of the affected clients and provided to any IRS officer or employee upon request.

distractors.A: Incorrect because § 10.29(b)(3) strictly requires informed consent to be confirmed in writing by each affected client within 30 days.
distractors.B: CORRECT: States the exact 30-day maximum window for written confirmation by each affected client (§ 10.29(b)(3)) and the 36-month retention period after conclusion of the representation (§ 10.29(c)).
distractors.C: Incorrect because the written consent is signed by each affected client (not the IRS Revenue Agent) within 30 days (not 60 days) and retained for 36 months after conclusion of the representation (not 12 months).
distractors.D: Incorrect because § 10.29(b) explicitly permits waiving a conflict of interest when all three conditions in (b)(1)–(3) are satisfied.
distractors.E: Incorrect because the written confirmation deadline is 30 days (not 90 days) and the retention period is 36 months (3 years) from the conclusion of the representation.

questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Marcus Vance is preparing an individual federal income tax return for a client who wants to claim an aggressive business deduction that is NOT a tax shelter or reportable transaction. After researching the Internal Revenue Code, Treasury regulations, and Tax Court precedent, Vance concludes that the deduction has approximately a 25% likelihood of being sustained on its merits—meaning it satisfies the 'Reasonable Basis' standard (~20% or higher) but falls short of 'Substantial Authority' (~40% or higher). In addition, the client hands Vance a handwritten summary of travel expenses that directly contradicts the client's bank statements. Under 31 CFR § 10.34(a), (c), and (d), under what conditions may Vance sign the return containing the deduction, and how must Vance handle the contradictory travel expense summary?

options.text: Vance may sign the return without disclosing the deduction because any non-frivolous position (>5% likelihood) is permissible without disclosure, and Vance may accept the client's handwritten travel summary without inquiry because preparers never verify client data.

Vance may sign the return containing the deduction ONLY if the position is adequately disclosed to the IRS (e.g., on Form 8275) because it has a Reasonable Basis (~25%) rather than Substantial Authority (~40%), must inform the client of potential penalties and the opportunity to avoid them through disclosure, and MUST make reasonable inquiries regarding the travel expenses because a practitioner may not ignore client-furnished information that appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete.
Vance is strictly prohibited from signing the return even with Form 8275 disclosure because every position on a tax return must meet the 'More Likely Than Not' (>50%) standard.

Vance may sign the return without disclosure if the client signs a hold-harmless waiver, but Vance must independently audit every single canceled check and receipt for all categories on the tax return.
Vance must require a 75% certainty level before signing any tax return and must report the contradictory travel summary to the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility.

questions.goldenQuote: The practitioner may not, however, ignore the implications of information furnished to, or actually known by, the practitioner, and must make reasonable inquiries if the information as furnished appears to be incorrect, inconsistent with an important fact or another factual assumption, or incomplete.
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.34 (Standards with respect to tax returns and documents)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Distinguish the confidence threshold required for an UNDISCLOSED tax position ('Substantial Authority') versus an ADEQUATELY DISCLOSED non-tax-shelter position ('Reasonable Basis'), and check the rule on client-furnished information.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.34 and read paragraphs (a)(1)-(2), (c), and (d).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): A non-tax-shelter position with a Reasonable Basis (~25%) can be signed ONLY if adequately disclosed (Form 8275). And under § 10.34(d), while a practitioner generally relies in good faith on client information without audit, the practitioner MUST make reasonable inquiries when the information appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.34(a) (incorporating IRC § 6694(a)(2)), a practitioner may not sign a tax return containing a non-tax-shelter position unless it either (1) has 'Substantial Authority' (~40% or greater likelihood of being sustained) if undisclosed, OR (2) has at least a 'Reasonable Basis' (~20% or greater likelihood) AND is adequately disclosed to the IRS on Form 8275 (or Form 8275-R). Since the position has a ~25% likelihood, it satisfies Reasonable Basis and may be signed only if adequately disclosed. Under § 10.34(c), Vance must also inform the client of potential penalties and the opportunity to avoid them through disclosure. Finally, under § 10.34(d), although a practitioner may generally rely in good faith without verification on client-furnished information, the practitioner may NOT ignore the implications of information known to the practitioner and MUST make reasonable inquiries when the furnished information appears incorrect, inconsistent with other facts, or incomplete.

distractors.A: Incorrect because an undisclosed position requires Substantial Authority (~40%), a mere 'non-frivolous' standard was replaced by 'Reasonable Basis' for disclosed positions, and § 10.34(d) prohibits ignoring contradictory client data.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately applies the Reasonable Basis + Adequate Disclosure (Form 8275) standard under § 10.34(a), the penalty disclosure rule under § 10.34(c), and the duty of reasonable inquiry for inconsistent client data under § 10.34(d).
distractors.C: Incorrect because the 'More Likely Than Not' (>50%) standard applies only to tax shelters and reportable transactions, not ordinary business deductions.
distractors.D: Incorrect because a client waiver cannot override Circular 230 § 10.34 standards, and § 10.34(d) does not require auditing unimpeached client figures that appear consistent and complete.
distractors.E: Incorrect because neither a 75% certainty threshold nor reporting a client to OPR exists under Circular 230 § 10.34.
